questions.q: Why does Salesforce enforce governor limits on Apex transactions?
options: Because the platform is multi-tenant, and one org's runaway code can't be allowed to consume shared infrastructure at the expense of every other org
Because Apex is an interpreted language and can't run efficient code
Because governor limits only apply to free Developer Edition orgs, not production orgs
Because Salesforce charges extra for any transaction that runs quickly
questions.explain: Multi-tenancy means many customers share the same servers and database, so governor limits exist to stop one org's code from starving the resources every other org depends on.

questions.q: What happens when a transaction crosses a governor limit, as opposed to simply running slowly?
options: The transaction is automatically queued and retried later
The transaction throws an exception and rolls back entirely, rather than just running longer
The transaction completes successfully but is logged as a warning
The platform silently raises the limit for that transaction
questions.explain: Crossing a governor limit isn't a performance degradation — it's a hard failure. The transaction throws an exception and the whole thing rolls back, which is why performance work on Salesforce is about staying inside boundaries, not just going faster.

questions.q: A user says a Lightning page "feels slow." What should you determine first?
options: Whether the slowness is in client-side network/rendering or in a server-side Apex transaction, since the diagnosis and fix differ completely
Immediately rewrite every trigger on the object, since triggers are always the cause
Assume it's a governor limit issue and increase the org's Apex CPU allocation
Nothing can be determined without first disabling all validation rules
questions.explain: "Slow" can mean client-side rendering, network latency, or server-side transaction time — each has a different cause and a different fix, so the first diagnostic step is narrowing down which one you're actually looking at.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the lesson's four common root causes of Salesforce performance problems?
options: Non-bulkified code written assuming one record at a time
Non-selective queries, or queries run inside a loop
Doing work synchronously that didn't need an immediate answer
Using Lightning Web Components instead of Visualforce
questions.explain: The component framework choice isn't one of the four common root causes this lesson lists — non-bulkified code, non-selective/looped queries, unnecessary synchronous work, and excess data volume per transaction are.

questions.q: How does this course's three-chapter structure build on itself?
options: Chapter 1 covers foundational vocabulary and limits, Chapter 2 covers measurement and diagnosis, and Chapter 3 applies that to real fixes
All three chapters cover the same material at increasing difficulty with no new concepts
Chapter 1 is about Apex, Chapter 2 is about Visualforce, and Chapter 3 is about Lightning Web Components
The chapters can be studied in any order since each is fully self-contained
questions.explain: The course is deliberately sequenced: Chapter 1 builds the vocabulary and foundational limits, Chapter 2 is about measuring and diagnosing with real tools, and Chapter 3 applies all of it to concrete fixes, ending in a case study.
